meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The things that will destroy America'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Roosevelt, with a citable page number: a letter of 10 January 1917, read to a preparedness congress in Washington that month while he argued for American entry into the war.

answer.label: Verified — a letter of 10 January 1917
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and unusually well cited for a Roosevelt line. He wrote it to S. Stanwood Menken, head of the National Security League, on 10 January 1917. The letter was read aloud in Washington on 26 January 1917 to the League’s Congress of Constructive Patriotism and printed in the Proceedings of that congress at page 172. Roosevelt was out of office, out of favour and campaigning hard for American entry into the war the citation ↗.

source.excerpt: The things that will destroy America are prosperity-at-any-price, peace-at-any-price, safety-first instead of duty-first, the love of soft living and the get-rich-quick theory of life.
trail: The Theodore Roosevelt Association’s quotation index — the standard sourced reference for his words — files it under ‘Americanism’ with a full citation: to S. S. Menken, 10 January 1917; read before the National Security League, Washington, 26 January 1917; Proceedings of the Congress of Constructive Patriotism (New York, 1917), p. 172 the index entry ↗.

The recipient checks out. S. Stanwood Menken was a New York lawyer who founded the National Security League in 1914 and chaired the committee running the January 1917 congress — a preparedness rally held in Washington on 25–27 January, weeks before America entered the war.

The letter itself survives: the Theodore Roosevelt Center’s digital library holds a record for a Roosevelt letter to Menken of this date. Two honest caveats — we verified the wording and the page number through the Association’s sourced index rather than by opening the 1917 Proceedings ourselves, and the reading in Washington was done on Roosevelt’s behalf, not by him the archive record ↗.
source.cutTag: Letter to S. Stanwood Menken, 10 January 1917
source.excerptNote: Note the hyphens. Roosevelt is not listing four vices; he is naming four slogans — ‘prosperity-at-any-price’, ‘peace-at-any-price’, ‘safety-first’ — and hyphenating them to mark them as somebody else’s catchphrases. ‘Safety first’ was a real and hugely successful industrial-safety campaign at the time, which is why he could expect the jab to land.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About Theodore Roosevelt
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt (1858–1919) was president from 1901 to 1909 and, by 1917, a private citizen with no office and enormous voice — writing letters, columns and speeches pushing a reluctant country towards war. He is one of the most misquoted Americans there is, partly because he wrote so much that almost any strenuous-sounding sentence seems plausible. That makes the properly sourced items worth holding on to: this one has a recipient, two dates and a page number.

misattribution.heading: What to watch for
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound and the citation is specific. The problems are cosmetic — and one of them changes the joke.

items.why: Almost every reprint gives ‘prosperity at any price, peace at any price, safety first’ without hyphens. The sourced text hyphenates them, because Roosevelt is quoting slogans back at the people who used them. Lose the hyphens and you lose the sneer.

It circulates cut off after ‘duty-first’, or with ‘peace-at-any-price’ quietly dropped — which is convenient, since that clause is the one that dates it to a specific argument about entering the First World War.

You will see it dated 10 January 1917 and 26 January 1917. Both are right: the first is when Roosevelt wrote the letter, the second is when it was read aloud at the Washington congress that printed it.

It gets quoted as timeless moral commentary on soft modern living. It was written to the head of the National Security League as an argument for universal military service and American entry into the war — ‘safety first’ meant staying out of it.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Roosevelt — a letter of 10 January 1917 to S. Stanwood Menken, read in Washington on 26 January and printed in the congress Proceedings, p. 172 the sourced citation ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Every generation hears it as a description of itself, which is the whole trick: four abstractions, no dates, no names, and a diagnosis that fits whatever the listener already suspects has gone soft.

The 1917 setting is sharper than that. Roosevelt had spent two years attacking President Wilson for keeping America out of the war, and had been refused a command of his own. ‘Peace-at-any-price’ was not a mood he disapproved of; it was the other side’s campaign position.
detailsBody: 10 January 1917: Roosevelt writes to S. Stanwood Menken, chairman of the committee running the Congress of Constructive Patriotism.
25–27 January 1917: the National Security League holds that congress in Washington, D.C., pressing for preparedness and universal service.
26 January 1917: the letter is read aloud to the meeting on Roosevelt’s behalf.
It is printed in the congress Proceedings later that year, at page 172 — which is why the citation is so precise.
6 April 1917: the United States declares war. Roosevelt asks to raise a volunteer division and is refused.
context.pull: 'Safety first' was not a mood he disapproved of. In January 1917 it was the other side's campaign position.
